title: The Dark Web Was Invented by the US Navy
titles: He Built a $1.2 Billion Black Market. Then Made One Mistake.
The Dark Web Was Invented by the US Navy
$3.36 Billion Was Hidden in a Popcorn Tin
description: The dark web wasn't invented by criminals. It was invented by the US Navy. This is the full history of the dark web: the first internet message in 1969, the Navy's secret onion routing project, Tor, Bitcoin, the $1.2 billion Silk Road, the $3.36 billion found in a popcorn tin, AlphaBay, Hydra, and how every one of its kings was caught.

scenes.say: On the first of October, 2013, a young man sat down at a table in a public library in San Francisco and opened his laptop. A few minutes later, two strangers behind him started a loud argument. He turned around to look. And that was the moment the FBI grabbed his computer.

visuals.ai: a small public library in San Francisco
an open laptop on a library table

scenes.say: On that screen was a website that had sold more than a billion dollars of illegal goods. Drugs, fake documents, hacking tools, all paid for with a new kind of money that nobody could easily trace.

visuals.ai: a gold coin with a B symbol

scenes.say: It was called the Silk Road. And it lived on a hidden part of the internet that most people had never even heard of. The dark web.

visuals.sub: Who built it, who got rich, who got caught

scenes.say: But here's the twist almost nobody knows. The technology that hid that website, and still hides millions of people today, wasn't invented by criminals. It was invented by the United States Navy.

search: United States Naval Research Laboratory building
US Navy aircraft carrier at sea
visuals.ai: a navy aircraft carrier at sea

scenes.say: This is the story of how a secret military project became the most famous hiding place on Earth, how one website turned it into a billion dollar empire, and how every one of its kings was eventually found.

To understand the dark web, we have to go back to the very first message ever sent over the internet. It was 1969. A student at the University of California in Los Angeles tried to send the word LOGIN to a computer at Stanford, 350 miles away.
He typed L, then O, and the system crashed. So the first message in internet history was just two letters. Lo.

That network, called ARPANET, was paid for by the American military. It was built to share information, not to hide it. Every computer had an address, every message said where it came from and where it was going.

visuals.ai: an old computer terminal with a keyboard

scenes.say: Decades later, the internet still works the same way. Every time you visit a website, your computer sends an address, a bit like the return address on an envelope. Your internet company sees it. The website sees it. And anyone watching the line in between can see it too.

visuals.ai: an envelope with a return address

scenes.say: For most people, that's fine. But imagine you're a spy, working in another country, sending reports home over the internet. Every message you send says exactly where you are.

In 1995, three researchers at the US Naval Research Laboratory in Washington had an idea. David Goldschlag, Michael Reed and Paul Syverson. What if a message could travel through several computers, each one knowing only a tiny part of the journey?

They called it onion routing. Your message is wrapped in layers of encryption, like the layers of an onion. It bounces through three random computers around the world. Each one peels off one layer, and passes it on.
The first computer knows who you are, but not where you're going. The last one knows where you're going, but not who you are. No single computer knows both. That was the magic.
But the Navy had a problem. If only American spies used this network, then anyone who saw the network being used would know it was an American spy. To hide in a crowd, you need a crowd.

visuals.ai: a huge crowd of people in a city

scenes.say: So they made a decision that sounds crazy for a military project. They gave it away. In 2002, a version called Tor, The Onion Router, went online as free software that anyone in the world could use.

visuals.ai: a software developer speaking at a conference

scenes.say: Two young programmers, Roger Dingledine and Nick Mathewson, built it with one of the Navy researchers. By the end of 2003, the whole network was run by just a dozen volunteer computers. In 2006 it became a non profit, and for years, a big part of its money still came from the American government.

visuals.ai: a small server in someone's home

scenes.say: Now, people often mix up two words. The deep web and the dark web. They're not the same thing.

The deep web is simply everything that search engines can't see. Your email inbox. Your bank account. Private company files. It's huge, much bigger than the normal internet, and almost all of it is completely boring.

visuals.ai: an iceberg with most of it under water
a bank website on a laptop

scenes.say: The dark web is a tiny corner of the deep web. Websites that can only be opened through Tor, with strange addresses ending in dot onion. In 2004, Tor added a feature that let websites hide too, not just visitors. The owner of a dot onion site could be anywhere in the world.

For a few years, it was mostly used by privacy fans, journalists and activists. But there was still one thing missing. Even if nobody could see you, how would you pay for anything without a bank seeing it?

visuals.ai: a journalist typing on a laptop

scenes.say: The answer arrived on the thirty first of October, 2008. An unknown person, using the name Satoshi Nakamoto, published a nine page paper describing a new kind of digital money. Bitcoin.

No bank. No government. Just a giant public record, shared by thousands of computers, that tracks every coin. The first bitcoins were created in January 2009. To this day, nobody knows for sure who Satoshi really is.

visuals.ai: a bronze statue with a reflective face

scenes.say: Now the dark web had everything it needed. Hidden websites. Hidden visitors. And money that didn't need a name. All it needed was someone to put the pieces together.

That someone was a twenty six year old from Austin, Texas, named Ross Ulbricht. He had studied physics, he loved the idea of a world without government control, and he was looking for something big to build.

visuals.ai: a young man with short hair, 2010s

scenes.say: In early 2011, he launched a website on the dark web. He named it after the ancient trade route between China and Europe. The Silk Road. And on day one, the first things for sale were magic mushrooms he had grown himself.

search: Silk Road ancient trade route map
visuals.ai: an old map of the ancient Silk Road

scenes.say: It worked like eBay for things you couldn't buy anywhere else. Sellers had ratings. Buyers left reviews. The website held the money until the package arrived. And the packages came through the normal post.

visuals.ai: parcels at a post office sorting centre

scenes.say: For a few months, almost nobody knew it existed. Then, in June 2011, a news website wrote an article about it. Overnight, thousands of new users arrived. And two powerful American senators demanded that it be shut down.

visuals.ai: a news article on a screen

scenes.say: Ross started calling himself the Dread Pirate Roberts, after a character in a film whose name was passed from one pirate to the next. The idea was perfect. If the name could be passed on, nobody could ever be sure who was behind it.

visuals.ai: an old painting of a pirate ship

scenes.say: The money was staggering. According to the FBI, between 2011 and 2013 the Silk Road handled about nine and a half million bitcoins in sales, worth around one point two billion dollars. Ross took a small cut of every sale. His commissions came to about eighty million dollars.
He lived quietly in San Francisco, renting a small room, using a fake name. His roommates had no idea that the man next door was running the biggest black market on the internet.

visuals.ai: a row of houses in San Francisco
a small room with a desk

scenes.say: Every police agency in America wanted the Dread Pirate Roberts. The FBI, the drug agency, homeland security, even the tax office. But how do you find someone on a network that was designed by the Navy to make finding people impossible?

search: FBI headquarters J. Edgar Hoover Building

scenes.say: The answer was surprisingly simple. You stop looking at the dark web, and you start looking at the normal internet. Because before he became famous, Ross had made a tiny mistake.

An investigator from the tax agency, Gary Alford, searched through old internet forums from early 2011. He found a user named altoid who had promoted the Silk Road when it was brand new. Months later, the same altoid had posted asking for programming help, and left his real email address.
The email address included his name. Ross Ulbricht. One careless message, written before he ever thought anyone would care, pointed straight at the most wanted man online.

The hunt had dark twists of its own. Prosecutors later said Ross had paid to have several people killed, people he thought were threatening his empire. No one was ever actually killed, and those charges were later dropped. And two federal agents working on the case were caught stealing bitcoin for themselves.

Then the agents planned the arrest. They needed him to be logged in, with his laptop open, so the evidence couldn't be locked away. So on that October afternoon, they followed him to the Glen Park library, waited, and staged a fake argument right behind him.
When he turned his head, an agent pulled the open laptop away. Everything was on it. The website, the accounts, and a diary of how he had built the whole thing.
In 2015, Ross Ulbricht was put on trial in New York. He was thirty one years old. The jury found him guilty on every charge.

search: Daniel Patrick Moynihan United States Courthouse
visuals.ai: a federal courthouse in New York

scenes.say: The judge gave him two life sentences plus forty years, with no chance of parole. She said she wanted to send a message to anyone thinking of building the next Silk Road.

visuals.ai: the bars of a prison cell

scenes.say: For almost ten years, he sat in prison. Many people thought the sentence was far too harsh for a website owner who hadn't been convicted of violence. A campaign called Free Ross collected hundreds of thousands of signatures.
And then, on the twenty first of January, 2025, the newly returned President Donald Trump gave him a full pardon. The man who built the Silk Road walked out of prison a free man.
But the Silk Road had one more secret. And it was hiding in a popcorn tin.

In 2012, a young man named James Zhong found a flaw in the Silk Road. By clicking the withdraw button many times in a row, very fast, he tricked the site into paying him again and again. He walked away with over fifty thousand bitcoins.

visuals.ai: a hand clicking a computer mouse

scenes.say: At the time, those coins were worth less than a million dollars. Nobody noticed. He kept quiet for almost ten years, while the price of bitcoin went up, and up, and up.

In November 2021, investigators raided his house in Gainesville, Georgia. They found the coins on tiny computer devices, hidden in a safe under the floor, and inside a popcorn tin in a bathroom cupboard. They were now worth three point three six billion dollars.

visuals.ai: a small city in Georgia, USA
a safe hidden in a floor

visuals.label: Billion dollars, in a popcorn tin
visuals.note: Seized November 2021, US Department of Justice

scenes.say: It was one of the biggest money seizures in American history. James Zhong was sentenced to one year and one day in prison.
Shutting down the Silk Road didn't kill the dark web. It made it bigger. Within weeks, copies appeared. Silk Road 2. Then dozens of others, each one promising to be safer than the last.

visuals.ai: a painting of a many-headed serpent

scenes.say: The biggest was AlphaBay. Started in late 2014, it grew to be many times larger than the Silk Road, with hundreds of thousands of users and over a billion dollars in trades. Its owner was a quiet Canadian named Alexandre Cazes, living a life of luxury in Thailand.

In July 2017, police around the world moved at once. Cazes was arrested in Bangkok. A week later, he was found dead in his cell. And at the same time, Dutch police had pulled off something incredible.
They had secretly taken over another dark web market called Hansa, and kept running it, quietly, for about a month. When AlphaBay's users fled to Hansa, the police were waiting. They were the market.

Then there was Hydra. A Russian language market that started in 2015 and became the biggest of them all. Seventeen million customer accounts, nineteen thousand sellers, and around five billion dollars in total sales.
In April 2022, German police found Hydra's servers inside Germany, seized them, and shut the market down. In December 2024, a court in Russia sentenced its operator to life in prison.
So is the dark web just a criminal supermarket? Not quite. Because the same tool that hid Ross Ulbricht has also protected people risking their lives.

During the Arab Spring in 2011, protesters used Tor to reach blocked websites and talk to the world. In 2013, the whistleblower Edward Snowden relied on it while revealing secret government surveillance.

visuals.ai: a huge protest in a city square
a young man speaking to a camera

scenes.say: Today, big news organisations like the BBC and the New York Times run their own dot onion websites, so that people in countries with censorship can still read the news. Millions of people use Tor every day, and most of them aren't criminals at all.
So what does the history of the dark web teach us? First. A tool is never good or evil. The same layers that hide a drug market also hide a journalist in danger.

lines: A tool is just a tool.

visuals.ai: an old hammer on a workbench

scenes.say: Second. Bitcoin was never truly anonymous. Every single coin leaves a permanent trail on a public record. That trail is exactly how investigators found James Zhong, ten years later.
And third. The technology was almost perfect. The people weren't. Ross Ulbricht wasn't caught by breaking the Navy's code. He was caught by one old forum post with his own email in it.
